questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Describe the work done by a physiotherapist lifting an exercise weight
questions.stem: A physiotherapist lifts a 4.0 kg exercise weight 0.50 m vertically. Which statement correctly describes the work done against gravity?

options.text: The work equals the weight of the mass multiplied by the height lifted, about 19.6 J.
The work equals the mass multiplied by the height, about 2.0 J.
options.misconception: omits g from the work calculation

options.text: The work equals zero, because the weight ends up at its original height.
options.misconception: thinks a return trip cancels the work done

options.text: The work equals the distance the physiotherapist walked while lifting the weight.
options.misconception: uses horizontal distance instead of the lift height

questions.explanation: Work against gravity is force times distance along that force, so W = m g h = 4.0 x 9.8 x 0.50 = 19.6 J. Leaving out g understates the result.
questions.hint: Work is force times distance along the force.

options.text: It quadruples, because kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed.

options.misconception: treats kinetic energy as linear in speed

options.text: It stays the same, because the mass of the leg has not changed.
options.misconception: believes only mass can affect kinetic energy

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is half the mass times the square of the speed, so doubling the speed multiplies the energy by four. Mass sets the scale but not how speed affects it.

questions.stem: A physiotherapist lifts a 15 kg treatment table through 0.40 m and then lowers it back to its original height. What is the net work done by gravity over the complete round trip, in joules?

questions.stem: A nurse carries a 20 kg laundry bag up a staircase from the basement to the ground floor and finds that the task feels harder than carrying the same bag along a flat corridor. Explain this using power.

answer.exemplar: Carrying the bag up a staircase raises its centre of mass, so the nurse does work against gravity on top of any work done against friction, and the total work for the same mass is greater than along a flat corridor. questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a fast heavy effort demands more power than a slow light one
questions.stem: A physiotherapist asks a patient to complete a resisted knee extension in two ways: slowly with a light band, or quickly with a heavy one. Explain why the two efforts are not equivalent even when the total work is the same.

answer.exemplar: The muscles do the same total work in both cases, since the same displacement is covered against the same overall resistance, but power is that work divided by the time taken. The quick, heavy effort packs the same work into a much shorter time and therefore demands a far higher power, which is why it feels so much harder and fatigues the patient quickly. The slow effort spreads the identical work over a longer time, so the power and the peak demand on the muscle are much lower.

questions.explanation: Power is work divided by time, so the same work delivered quickly demands a much higher rate. The fast heavy effort therefore loads the muscle far more intensely than the slow light one.
questions.hint: Same work, different time, different power.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a resistance equipment power rating means during a pull
questions.stem: A physiotherapist hands a patient a therapy band and asks for a steady pull. Explain what the power rating of the resistance equipment means during that pull.

answer.exemplar: Power is the rate of doing work, so during a steady pull the rating tells the clinician how quickly the equipment is supplying energy to the patient. For a band pulled a fixed distance in a fixed time, the work is the mean pull times the stretch, and the power is that work divided by the time taken. A harder or faster pull raises the power, and the patient must supply energy at that rate from their muscles, which is why the effort tracks the power rather than the stretch alone.

questions.explanation: The rating is the rate at which work is done, which depends on the force and how quickly the pull is made. The patient must supply energy at that rate.
questions.hint: Power is a rate, so consider both force and speed.

questions.stem: A patient on a treadmill reaches a running speed and then the treadmill is switched to a steep incline at the same speed. Explain what happens to the patient's kinetic energy and why the effort still increases.

answer.exemplar: The patient's speed is unchanged, and kinetic energy depends only on mass and the square of speed, so the kinetic energy stays exactly the same. What changes is the energy balance: the incline means the patient must now also lift their body against gravity at a steady rate, so the treadmill motor must supply extra power while the kinetic energy is unchanged. The patient therefore works harder at the same speed even though their stored kinetic energy has not moved.

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed alone, so it is unchanged when the speed is unchanged. The extra effort comes from lifting against gravity.
questions.hint: Kinetic energy ignores the incline entirely.
